extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics studying or attempting to represent water (in the manner of Turner)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for representing water (calm surfaces, reflections, ripples, torrents, and falls) in landscape painting, with examples drawn from Turner's practice. Focuses on optical truth, compositional effects, texture, and the correct rendering of motion and history of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual exclusivity of surface and reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot, by any effort, see both the surface-details (near objects on the water) and the distant reflections together with equal clearness; the eye must adopt either a surface focus or a distant/reflection focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of looking at duckweed vs. the cloud reflections: if you look for reflection you adapt to great distance and near leaves become vague; if you look for the leaves you adapt to near rays and reflections melt into vague flashing. Therefore a painting that gives reflections with the same clearness as surface details presupposes an effort of the eye and destroys the sensation of surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflections on distant water appear distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: On the distant surface of water, all reflections will be seen plainly because the same focus that receives distant objects also receives rays reflected from distant water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reflection of Mont Blanc on the Lake of Geneva is visible without effort because the water is itself a mile off. When painting distant lakes/expanses, give reflected crags and hills with fidelity and distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rendering near reflections with full distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving a perfect, distinct image of near reflected objects implies looking under the surface and so destroys the sense of the surface; near reflections should often be confused and mixed, except at the very water-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Vandevelde: a perfect image of his ship would have required the eye to look under the water and would have lost surface feeling. Instead, near reflections should be vivid in colour but unintelligible in form so the eye rests on the polished surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render marginal reflections clearly, distant-object reflections vaguely
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary effect of water is achieved by giving the reflections of the margin (objects close to the water-line) clear and distinct, while reflections of distant objects should be vague and indistinct in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The margin is often so clearly mirrored that it is hard to tell where water begins; but when touching reflections of high trees or clouds, drawing must become vague and uncertain while remaining vivid in hue and light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflections are rearranged views, not duplicates
rubrics_metrics.description: The reflection of near objects is not an exact copy of the parts seen above the water, but a different view and arrangement—often showing different sides, lights, or elements that are invisible from the bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dark sides of leaves may appear in the reflection though the light sides are seen above; some bank objects are lost in reflection while others appear only below. Artists who duplicate above-and-below exactly destroy the essence of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use altered tonality/opposition in reflections to sustain surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Change tones and oppositions between the above-water scene and its reflection so that reflected elements have their own character and do not merely mock the reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's Nottingham example: the reflected sign-post is relieved against the illumined summit rather than the dark base, altering its perceived tone (white above becomes dark gray in reflection). Such deliberate tonal alteration keeps the eye on the surface as an element in its own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep reflections suggestive rather than literal ('say everything, yet say nothing too plainly')
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of water painting consists in making reflections characterful and evidently derived from definite forms while remaining uncertain and inexplicable enough to preserve the sensation of surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflections should give an immediate sense of brightness and atmosphere yet resist literal interpretation so the viewer does not 'plunge' into the reflection; this is a compositional and perceptual aim, not just optical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create delicate surface texture for calm water
rubrics_metrics.description: Calm water surfaces require a peculiar texture—delicate tints and sometimes crumbling dry-brush touches—that give an appearance of substantial liquidity and prevent pale passages from looking papery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner achieves this by a modification of body colour plus dry brushwork that shows through; attempts to copy this mechanically by ordinary body colour often fail. Best example: distance of the Devonport with the Dockyards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit local colour and observed detail to produce radiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use faithfully observed local colours and particulars (e.g., Venetian painted sails) to elicit radiance and vivid effect from the composition, especially where reflections do not assist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Sun of Venice, Turner uses the bright painted sails and grotesque vanes to create a central blaze of colour and radiance; such truthful detail can substitute for reflective information when the water surface is large and blank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate past agitation or hidden current by small incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in scenes of placid surface, include trifling incidents (e.g., separated reflections, zigzag lines) to report previous commotion or present stirring of tide/current that the stillness alone would not show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowes example: three spaced black strokes for a distant buoy indicate vast swell spacing and impart a sense of latent power and history to the calm scene. Such details can be central to the composition's feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate river tranquility from current by wakes and stream patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent whether a wide river is calm like a lake or a majestic current by rendering wakes, dividing flows, and localized undulations that indicate the stream's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loire example: show the stream dividing at a boat's bow into long dark waves and breaking reflected sunlight by the boat's wake so the viewer understands it's a flowing current, not a mere still surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict contrary waves from recoil against shore
rubrics_metrics.description: When wakes strike shores and rebound, portray the resultant contrary waves and their interactions with surges to explain local disorder in the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides narrative and physical plausibility: the point of interaction should be visible (e.g., sudden subdivision of waves, vertical spring of spray) so viewers can account for the wave patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render complex interactions of wakes and shore (reverted waves and spray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give not just the primary wake lines but also their intersections with shore and other surges, including reverted weaker surges and points where spray springs up vertically where lines cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confluence of Seine and Marne: Turner paints both receding surges and their rebound on the shore, marking intersections by subdivisions and vertical spray; such thoroughness makes the disturbance intelligible and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show ripple-plus-sun phenomena via multitudinous small reflections (centre gleam)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ripples can create brilliant gleams (a bright central passage) not possible on calm water, because innumerable small faces on ripples reflect the sun; represent bright and dark parts as reflections (not shadows/light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loch Lomond vignette: the centre gleam is due to multitudinous reflection of the sun on ripple sides; dark parts are cloud reflections, bright parts are sun reflections—render accordingly and ensure surface shows rippled texture underlying apparent light-and-shade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate observer height by loss of bank reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: The height of the viewpoint should be expressed by the disappearance of bank reflections across the broad surface: from a high vantage we see only a narrow dark line under steep banks, the rest reflecting sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In distant river drawings (e.g., Caudebec), Turner gives only a narrow line of dark water under the precipice and lets the broad surface reflect sky, thus indicating vantage height through reflection loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine water surface and mist distinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: When water surfaces are associated with mist, render the mingling so that promontories, clouds and lake surfaces melt into each other appropriately—sometimes showing the lake as a field of low white mist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swiss drawings: examples include lake surfaces covered with low white mist or lake surfaces appearing like fallen moonlight cloud; treat such passages to convey atmosphere and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render falling water to express weight by concentric catenary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: High falls should be drawn with concentric zones and delicate curves (catenary forms) emphasizing plunge and weight, not merely parabolic springing lines or shapeless foam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's Upper Fall of the Tees shows concentric zones and curves that express a powerful stream descending and expanding; show form beneath spray and avoid hiding definitive falling shapes in indiscriminate foam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parabolic 'leap' forms for great waterfalls—depict plunge
rubrics_metrics.description: Where water truly tumbles over great heights, do not use springing/parabolic lines which make the stream look active/wiry; instead render catenary/plunging lines conveying prostration and ponderous fall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction: small weirs show spring/parabolic shapes; large falls require loss of spring and adoption of plunging catenary lines—this is essential to make observers feel weight and wildness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate interrupted vs continuous streams in form and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrupted streams (many pools/leaps) present a succession of leaps, parabolic splashes and glassy pools; continuous torrents (uninterrupted slope or flood) take the shape of their bed—smooth domes, deep undulating curves, and no regular foam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrupted stream: pauses, curdles, leaps into pools. Continuous torrent: gains impetus, clears obstacles in smooth domes, bends into parallel lines by velocity, curves alternate convex/concave and present united motion—use these distinctions when composing and drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render continuous torrents with exquisite curved lines and little foam
rubrics_metrics.description: Torrents with sustained impetus form beautiful undulating curved lines (modulations from convex to concave), often foamless except where bed geometry forces breakers; these lines are the exclusive attribute of mountain-torrents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Llanthony Abbey example: huge greenish unbroken oceanic curves bending into each other, jets of spray along rocky shore; draw every fine form with careful chiaroscuro of delicate grays and greens to express rapidity, force and refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use refined chiaroscuro and color to render torrent forms and vivid foam
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply studied chiaroscuro of delicate colour (grays and greens) and refined execution to render torrent surfaces and the vividness of foam through middle tints rather than crude highlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's torrents show unity of motion, refined color, and vivid foam that emerges from general middle tone; aim for that refinement rather than coarse bright highlights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict interrupted torrents' quiet pools with glassy reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a stream pauses into quiet glassy pools, render these with unstirred, perfect images (e.g., of drinking cattle) set within the larger active movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mercury and Argus: the torrent in foreground stops twice in quiet pools with exact reflections. Use such contrasts (glassy pools amid motion) to enrich narrative and variation in water treatment.
